citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

derivations.claim: For $q,k\ge1$ set $\phi(q,k)=\frac{(q+k-2)(q+k-1)}2+q$. Listing pairs by increasing $q+k$ and then increasing $q$ shows that $\phi$ is a bijection. Each digit $D_j$ lies in $\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$, and prescribing the first $N$ consecutive digits specifies exactly one half-open interval of length $b^{-N}$ by [F1]. More generally, prescribing any $s$ distinct digit positions among the first $N$ leaves exactly $b^{N-s}$ such intervals, so those digits have joint probability $b^{-s}$.

Fix distinct $q_1,\ldots,q_s$ and positive integers $n_1,\ldots,n_s$. The index sets $\{\phi(q_i,k):1\le k\le n_i\}$ are disjoint. If their digit values are prescribed, let $N$ be the largest used index. Exactly $b^{N-\sum_i n_i}$ length-$b^{-N}$ intervals have those values, so their joint probability is $b^{-\sum_i n_i}$. For each $q$ and $m\ge1$, the event $T_{q,m}=\{D_{\phi(q,k)}=b-1\text{ for every }k\ge m\}$ is contained, for every $L\ge1$, in the event that its first $L$ tail digits all equal $b-1$. Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb P(T_{q,m})\le b^{-L}$ for every $L$, so [F5] gives $\mathbb P(T_{q,m})=0$. The countable union of these events over $q,m$ is null. Outside it, each stream has no tail consisting entirely of $b-1$ digits; consequently a prescribed initial digit word places its numeric sum in the corresponding half-open base-$b$ interval, not at its right endpoint. Thus every finite family of the numeric $\widetilde U_{q_i}$ has the product uniform cylinder probabilities outside a null set. The event $\widetilde U_q=1$ is contained in $T_{q,1}$, so replacing that value by $0$ leaves every finite-dimensional law unchanged.

Each digit $D_j$ is constant on the finite Borel partition into intervals of length $b^{-j}$. A finite partial sum defining $\widetilde U_q$ is constant on the common refinement at the largest digit index it uses, hence is measurable. Its pointwise limit is measurable by [F4]. The map $g:[0,1]\to[0,1)$ given by $g(x)=x$ for $x<1$ and $g(1)=0$ is Borel; explicitly, for Borel $A\subseteq[0,1)$, $g^{-1}(A)=(A\cap[0,1))$ together with $\{1\}$ exactly when $0\in A$. Therefore $U_q=g(\widetilde U_q)$ is measurable. For any finite set of indices $q_i$, the $b$-adic cylinder rectangles for $(U_{q_i})$ form a $\pi$-system generating the Borel sets of $[0,1)^s$: every open set is the union of the countably many such cells contained in it, since the cell diameters tend to zero. Step 2.1 gives agreement there with product Lebesgue measure; [F2] therefore gives the product law on all Borel sets. Hence the $U_q$ are mutually independent and each is uniform.

Each map $u\mapsto\sigma_{\min\{b!-1,\lfloor b!u\rfloor\}}$ is Borel, with the preimage of $\sigma_r$ equal to $[r/b!,(r+1)/b!)$ for $0\le r<b!$. For distinct $q_1,\ldots,q_s$, independence and uniformity from step 3.1 give $\mathbb P(\pi_{q_i}=\sigma_{r_i}\text{ for every }i)=\prod_i\mathbb P(U_{q_i}\in[r_i/b!,(r_i+1)/b!))=(b!)^{-s}$. These maps are measurable and the joint probabilities show that the $\pi_q$ are mutually independent uniform permutations.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal A_b$ be the algebra of finite unions of base-$b$ elementary boxes in $[0,1)^d$. There are countably many such boxes. For any open $O\subseteq[0,1)^d$ and $x\in O$, choose $\delta_x>0$ such that the relative $\delta_x$-ball about $x$ lies in $O$. At every sufficiently large level $k$, the unique level-$k$ box containing $x$ has diameter at most $\sqrt d\,b^{-k}<\delta_x$, hence is contained in $O$. Therefore $O$ is the union of the countably many base-$b$ boxes contained in it. Thus $\sigma(\mathcal A_b)$ contains every open set and equals the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.

Let $\mathcal C$ be the Borel sets $E$ for which every $\eta>0$ admits $A\in\mathcal A_b$ with $\lambda(E\triangle A)<\eta$. It contains $\mathcal A_b$ and is closed under complements and finite unions by the symmetric-difference inequalities and the algebra property. If $E_i\in\mathcal C$, then $E^{(N)}=\bigcup_{i=1}^N E_i\uparrow E=\bigcup_{i\ge1}E_i$; [F2] lets us choose $N$ with $\lambda(E\setminus E^{(N)})<\eta/2$. Approximate each of the finitely many $E_i$, $i\le N$, within $\eta/(2N)$ and union those approximants. The resulting member of $\mathcal A_b$ is within $\eta$ of $E$. Thus $\mathcal C$ is a $\sigma$-algebra, so step 1.1 gives $\mathcal C$ equal to all Borel sets.

By [F1], choose a finite simple function $s=\sum_{j=1}^M c_j\mathbf1_{E_j}$ with $\|f-s\|_2<\varepsilon/2$. By step 2.1 choose $A_j\in\mathcal A_b$ so that $\sum_{j=1}^M |c_j|\lambda(E_j\triangle A_j)^{1/2}<\varepsilon/2$. The finite box step function $g=\sum_j c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ then satisfies $\|s-g\|_2\le\sum_j|c_j|\|\mathbf1_{E_j}-\mathbf1_{A_j}\|_2 =\sum_j|c_j|\lambda(E_j\triangle A_j)^{1/2}<\varepsilon/2$.
The triangle inequality gives $\|f-g\|_2\le\|f-s\|_2+\|s-g\|_2<\varepsilon$. Since $f$ and $\varepsilon$ were arbitrary, the stated finite-span density follows.

Let $b\ge2$ and $d\ge1$. For $k\ge0$ and $0\le t<b^k$, put
$I_{k,t}=[tb^{-k},(t+1)b^{-k})$. For $1\le r<b$, define the normalized
base-$b$ Haar contrast
$$h_{k,t,r}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{b^{k+1}}{r(r+1)}}\left( \sum_{c=0}^{r-1}\mathbf1_{I_{k+1,bt+c}}(x) -r\mathbf1_{I_{k+1,bt+r}}(x)\right).$$

For a nonempty subset $u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let
$\kappa=(k_j)_{j\in u}$, $\tau=(t_j)_{j\in u}$ with
$0\le t_j<b^{k_j}$, and $\rho=(r_j)_{j\in u}$ with $1\le r_j<b$. Set
$$\psi_{u,\kappa,\tau,\rho}(x)=\prod_{j\in u}h_{k_j,t_j,r_j}(x_j).$$
For a real Borel function $f\in L^2([0,1)^d)$, define
$$I(f)=\int_{[0,1)^d}f(x)\,dx,\qquad \nu_{u,\kappa}(f)=\sum_{\tau,\rho} \left(\int_{[0,1)^d}f(x)\psi_{u,\kappa,\tau,\rho}(x)\,dx\right) \psi_{u,\kappa,\tau,\rho},\qquad \sigma^2_{u,\kappa}(f)=\int_{[0,1)^d}\nu_{u,\kappa}(f)^2\,dx.$$
The sums defining each $\nu_{u,\kappa}$ are finite. The complete orthogonal
decomposition across all $u,\kappa$ is established separately.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $n\ge1$, let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with $a_j<b_j$, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel. If $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $f\in L^1(\lambda_n|_Q)$ and its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $u$ is the full coordinate set, then $f_u=f$ and $\partial_u f_u=\partial_u f$. Otherwise, [F6] makes $f_u$ continuous: changing $x_u$ by less than $\delta$ changes the integrand uniformly in $x_{-u}$, and integration over a unit-volume cube preserves that bound. Repeated application of [F2] to the complementary coordinates, with [F4] identifying iterated integrals and [A1, F5] identifying the Riemann and Lebesgue integrals, gives $\partial_u f_u(x_u)=\int_{[0,1]^{d-|u|}}\partial_u f(x_u,x_{-u})\,dx_{-u}$. The same uniform-continuity argument makes this derivative continuous. Since $|\partial_u f|$ is continuous on the nonempty compact cube, [F7] gives a finite supremum; the displayed integral (or $f_u=f$ in the full-set case) shows $M_u\le\sup_{[0,1]^d}|\partial_u f|$.

Fix $(\tau,\rho)$ and let $c_{u,\kappa,\tau,\rho}=\int f_u(x_u)\prod_{j\in u}h_{k_j,t_j,r_j}(x_j)\,dx_u$. The integrand is bounded and continuous on each cell of a finite rectangular partition, so it is Riemann integrable; by [A1, F5] this coefficient is also its Riemann integral. Each contrast has integral zero on its parent. Subtracting the left-endpoint value in one coordinate therefore leaves the integral unchanged. For a nonempty subset $u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let

$0\le t_j<b^{k_j}$, and $\rho=(r_j)_{j\in u}$ with $1\le r_j<b$. Set

$$I(f)=\int_{[0,1)^d}f(x)\,dx,\qquad \nu_{u,\kappa}(f)=\sum_{\tau,\rho} \left(\int_{[0,1)^d}f(x)\psi_{u,\kappa,\tau,\rho}(x)\,dx\right) \psi_{u,\kappa,\tau,\rho},\qquad \sigma^2_{u,\kappa}(f)=\int_{[0,1)^d}\nu_{u,\kappa}(f)^2\,dx.$$
The sums defining each $\nu_{u,\kappa}$ are finite. The complete orthogonal
decomposition across all $u,\kappa$ is established separately.

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

$[0,1)^d$. The array is **marginally uniform** if every $X_i$ has normalized

**RQMC design** consists of marginal uniformity together with a separately
stated low-discrepancy condition. For a family indexed by $n$, one such
condition is an almost-sure bound $D_n^*(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\le\delta_n$ with
deterministic $\delta_n\to0$, where $D_n^*$ is the star discrepancy of
[[def-star-discrepancy-and-digital-net]]. For a fixed $n$, an exact net-count
property may instead be declared; no star-discrepancy rate follows merely
from marginal uniformity.

For a Borel function $f$ integrable on the cube, set
$$I(f)=\int_{[0,1)^d}f(x)\,dx,\qquad \widehat I_n(f)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i).$$
An **independent full-set randomization** is an independent copy of the whole
vector $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$. Independence is across copies, not among points
within one copy. The point count $n$ and number of independent
randomizations $R$ are separate parameters.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be a marginally uniform randomized point array in
$[0,1)^d$, with no independence assumption among its points. For every Borel
$f\in L^1([0,1)^d)$, the RQMC estimator
$\widehat I_n(f)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ is integrable and
$$\mathbb E[\widehat I_n(f)]=\int_{[0,1)^d}f(x)\,dx.$$

Fix the observed data and an integrable RQMC target $I=I(f)$. Suppose one
full-set randomization produces an estimator $\widehat I$ with
$\mathbb E[\widehat I]=I$ and finite variance $\tau^2$. For $R\ge2$
independent full-set randomizations, write their IID estimates as
$\widehat I_1,\ldots,\widehat I_R$ and their mean as
$\overline I_R=R^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^R\widehat I_r$. Then
$$\widehat V_R=\frac1{R(R-1)} \sum_{r=1}^R(\widehat I_r-\overline I_R)^2$$
is unbiased for $\operatorname{Var}(\overline I_R)=\tau^2/R$. This variance
is over computation randomization conditional on the fixed data and rule; it
does not include data-sampling variation.

Assume AC. Let $(Z_r)_{r\ge1}$ be IID real computation-replicate outputs with mean $\mu$ and variance $0<\tau^2<\infty$. Then, as $R\to\infty$,
$$\frac{\sqrt R(\overline Z_R-\mu)}{\tau}\Rightarrow N(0,1),\qquad\overline Z_R:=\frac1R\sum_{r=1}^{R}Z_r.$$
This is a limit for the replicate-randomization law under the stated fixed-target setup; it is not a data-sampling confidence statement and does not by itself justify a finite-$R$ Student interval.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, and write $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$. For $n\ge2$, define $s_n^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2$. Then $s_n^2\to\sigma^2$ almost surely. If $\sigma^2>0$, then $\widehat{se}_n/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\to1$ almost surely.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$a_{i,j}=\sum_{k\ge1}a_{i,j,k}b^{-k},\qquad a_{i,j,k}\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}.$$

$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let

$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
